body:
In Galatians, it is striking how Paul struggles with this community. He is angry, frustrated, and does not hesitate to tell them exactly what he thinks.

“Are you so stupid? After beginning with the Spirit, are you now ending with the flesh?”

Those are strong words. But why is Paul so upset?

The Galatians had received the Gospel. Christ crucified had been proclaimed to them, and they had received the Holy Spirit through faith. Yet they were now being persuaded that following the Jewish Law was necessary to complete what Christ had already accomplished.

Paul's frustration begins to make sense. They had begun with the Spirit, yet were now relying on their own religious efforts rather than trusting in the grace of God.

And I wonder how often we do the same.

We believe in God, profess our faith, and try to live according to His teachings. Yet when difficulties arise, how quickly do we begin relying on ourselves, trying to control the outcome rather than trusting in the One who knows what we need?

Then we come to today's Gospel, where Jesus teaches us about the persistence of prayer.

“Ask and you will receive; seek and you will find; knock and the door will be opened to you.”

He then asks what father, when his son asks for a fish, would give him a snake instead? Or when asked for an egg, would give him a scorpion?

Of course not. A loving father would never intentionally give his child something harmful in place of something good.

And that is precisely Jesus' point.

If we, with all our human imperfections, know how to give good gifts to those we love, how much more does our heavenly Father?

But Jesus takes it one step further.

“How much more will the Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?”

The Holy Spirit.

Not necessarily the answer we were expecting. Jesus doesn't promise that everything we ask for will happen exactly as we desire. Instead, He directs us toward something far greater. The Father desires to give us His very Spirit.

And suddenly, these two readings come together.

Paul is asking the Galatians why they have turned away from relying on the Holy Spirit, while Jesus is telling us to continue asking the Father for that very gift.

How often do we hear someone say, “Pray about it”? Say a Rosary. Begin a novena. Ask your guardian angel for help. There are so many ways we are encouraged to pray, and Jesus tells us to keep asking, seeking, and knocking.

But why must we persevere if God already knows what we need?

Is it because God needs convincing? Do we have to pray enough times before He will listen?

Of course not.

Our Father already loves us. Yet something happens when we continue returning to Him, especially when prayer seems quiet and the answers do not come.

What begins as a prayer for a particular outcome can gradually become a prayer for the strength to accept something entirely different.

And that is the difficult part.

We pray for healing, relief, direction, and the people we love. Naturally, we hope God will answer in the way we believe is best. But what happens when He doesn't?

Do we become discouraged? Do we stop asking? Or do we continue trusting Him, even when we cannot understand what He is doing?

Jesus assures us that the Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. Maybe that is what we need most when the answers are slow in coming. Not simply a change in our circumstances, but the Holy Spirit who gives us the strength to remain faithful within them.

Trusting God's will does not mean everything will unfold without pain or disappointment. It means believing He remains faithful, even when we cannot see beyond what is happening today.

So continue to pray. Continue to ask, seek, and knock. Not because the Father is reluctant to hear you, but because He loves you and desires to draw you closer to Himself.

And when the answer is not what you hoped for, ask Him for the grace to trust what you cannot yet understand.

After all, if we began our journey with the Holy Spirit, why would we ever try to finish it without Him?
opening: Beginning with the Spirit, Continuing in Trust
prayer: Heavenly Father,  You know my needs before I even speak them, yet You invite me to keep asking, seeking, and knocking. When my prayers seem unanswered, help me not to lose heart. Give me the Holy Spirit to guide my thoughts, strengthen my faith, and teach me to trust Your will rather than my own. When I cannot understand Your ways, remind me that Your love has not changed. May I never turn away from the Spirit who first led me to You.  Amen.
theme: What happens when we begin with faith but struggle to trust God with the outcome?
title: Let Go, Let Jesus
